exercises.title: The board
exercises.text: Chess is played on an 8×8 board. Columns are files, named a to h. Rows are ranks, numbered 1 to 8. Every square is named file first, then rank: this one is e4.

exercises.title: Find e4
exercises.prompt: Tap the e4 square.
exercises.good: That is e4: the e-file, 4th rank.
exercises.bad: Find the e-file first (5th column), then go up to rank 4.

exercises.title: Find d5
exercises.prompt: Tap the d5 square.
exercises.good: Right. d5 is one of the four centre squares.
exercises.bad: d is the 4th file. Count up to the 5th rank.

exercises.title: Find h1
exercises.prompt: Tap the h1 square.
exercises.good: h1: White's bottom-right corner.
exercises.bad: h is the last file on the right, and rank 1 is White's first row.

exercises.title: Light or dark?
exercises.prompt: The square in each player's bottom-right corner is always light. What colour is h1?
exercises.good: Light. If the board is set up with a dark square there, turn it round.
exercises.bad: Look at the bottom-right corner of the board.

exercises.title: The starting position
exercises.text: Each side starts with 8 pawns, 2 rooks, 2 knights, 2 bishops, a queen and a king. White always moves first. The queen starts on her own colour: the white queen on the light d1 square.

exercises.title: Find the queen
exercises.prompt: Tap the white queen.
exercises.good: The white queen starts on d1, a light square.
exercises.bad: The queen has the crown with points. She sits next to the king.

exercises.title: Find a knight
exercises.prompt: Tap one of the black knights.
exercises.good: Knights start next to the rooks, on b8 and g8 for Black.
exercises.bad: Knights look like a horse. Black's pieces are on the far side.

exercises.title: The rook
exercises.text: The rook moves any number of squares in a straight line: up, down, left or right. It can't jump over pieces.

exercises.title: Rook moves
exercises.prompt: Tap any square the rook on d4 can move to.
exercises.good: Yes. The rook covers its whole file and rank.
exercises.bad: Rooks only move in straight lines along the file or rank.

exercises.title: Rook capture
exercises.prompt: Capture the black pawn with your rook.
exercises.good: Rooks capture by moving onto the enemy piece.
exercises.bad: The pawn is on the same file as your rook.

exercises.title: The bishop
exercises.text: The bishop moves any number of squares diagonally. A bishop stays on its starting colour for the whole game.

exercises.title: Bishop moves
exercises.prompt: Tap a square the bishop can move to. Your own pawn is in the way on one side.
exercises.good: Right. The pawn on d2 blocks the other diagonal.
exercises.bad: Bishops move diagonally and can't pass through their own pieces.

exercises.title: Bishop capture
exercises.prompt: Win the black rook.
exercises.good: The long diagonal was open all the way to g7.
exercises.bad: Follow the diagonal from b2 up to the right.

exercises.title: Which piece?
exercises.prompt: Which of these pieces moves diagonally?
exercises.good: Bishops move on diagonals, rooks on straight lines.
exercises.bad: One moves in straight lines, the other on diagonals.

exercises.title: The queen
exercises.text: The queen moves like a rook and a bishop combined: any number of squares in a straight line or diagonally. She is your strongest piece.

exercises.title: Queen capture
exercises.prompt: Capture the rook with your queen.
exercises.good: The diagonal d1–h5 was open.
exercises.bad: Look along the diagonal from d1 toward the right.

exercises.title: Queen moves
exercises.prompt: Tap a square the queen on c3 can move to.
exercises.good: The queen reaches files, ranks and diagonals.
exercises.bad: Straight lines and diagonals from c3. The pawn on c5 blocks part of the file.

exercises.title: The king
exercises.text: The king moves one square in any direction. It is slow, but the whole game is about it: if your king is trapped, you lose.

exercises.title: Safe squares
exercises.prompt: A king can never move onto an attacked square. Which king move is legal?
exercises.good: Kf1 is the only one of these not attacked by the rook.
exercises.bad: The rook on d2 attacks the whole 2nd rank.

exercises.title: King capture
exercises.prompt: The black queen is next to your king and nothing defends it. Take it.
exercises.good: Kings can capture too, as long as the piece isn't defended.
exercises.bad: Your king can step onto d2.

exercises.title: The knight
exercises.text: The knight moves in an L: two squares one way, then one square to the side. It is the only piece that can jump over others.

exercises.title: Knight moves
exercises.prompt: Tap a square the knight can jump to.
exercises.good: From the edge a knight has fewer jumps.
exercises.bad: Two squares in one direction, then one to the side.

exercises.title: Win the queen
exercises.prompt: Your knight can take the queen. Do it.
exercises.good: Knights are great at catching queens off guard.
exercises.bad: Try the L-shape from d4 toward c6.

exercises.title: Count the jumps
exercises.prompt: How many squares can this knight reach?
exercises.good: Eight. A knight in the centre is at its strongest.
exercises.bad: Count every L-shape from d4.

exercises.title: Jump over
exercises.prompt: Your pawns are in the way, but knights jump. Take the rook.
exercises.good: Pieces in between never stop a knight.
exercises.bad: The rook on c3 is one L-jump from b1.

exercises.title: Pawns
exercises.text: Pawns move straight forward one square. On its very first move a pawn may move two squares. Pawns never move backwards.

exercises.title: First move
exercises.prompt: Move the pawn two squares forward.
exercises.good: A two-square first move.
exercises.bad: From e2, a pawn may go straight to e4 on its first move.

exercises.title: Pawn captures
exercises.text: A pawn captures one square diagonally forward, never straight ahead.

exercises.title: Capture
exercises.prompt: Capture the black pawn.
exercises.good: Pawns capture diagonally.
exercises.bad: The black pawn is diagonally in front of yours.

exercises.title: Blocked
exercises.prompt: Can the white pawn on e4 move?
exercises.good: No. It can't capture straight ahead, so a pawn facing another pawn is stuck.
exercises.bad: Pawns move forward but capture diagonally. What is in front of it?

exercises.title: Promotion
exercises.text: A pawn that reaches the far rank turns into a queen, rook, bishop or knight. You almost always choose a queen.

exercises.title: Promote
exercises.prompt: Push the pawn to the last rank.
exercises.good: A new queen. That is a huge gain.
exercises.bad: One step forward to e8.

exercises.title: Rook capture
exercises.prompt: Take the black rook.
exercises.good: The a-file was wide open.
exercises.bad: Your rook and the black rook share a file.

exercises.title: Knight capture
exercises.prompt: Take the bishop with your knight.
exercises.good: Nice jump.
exercises.bad: One L-jump from f3 lands on e5.

exercises.title: Bishop moves
exercises.prompt: Tap a square the bishop on b2 can move to.
exercises.good: Correct.
exercises.bad: Diagonals only, and your pawn blocks one of them.

exercises.title: Most valuable
exercises.prompt: Not counting the king, which piece is worth the most?
exercises.good: The queen is worth about 9 pawns, a rook 5, a knight 3.
exercises.bad: Which piece combines two others?

exercises.title: Promote
exercises.prompt: Make a new queen.
exercises.good: Promoted.
exercises.bad: Push the pawn one square.

exercises.title: King capture
exercises.prompt: The knight is next to your king and undefended. Take it.
exercises.good: The king can capture any undefended neighbour.
exercises.bad: Step onto e2.

exercises.title: Check
exercises.text: When a king is attacked it is in check. The player in check must get out of it on the very next move.

exercises.title: Check or not?
exercises.prompt: Is the black king in check?
exercises.good: Yes. The bishop on b5 attacks e8 along the diagonal.
exercises.bad: Trace the bishop's diagonals from b5.

exercises.title: Three ways out
exercises.text: There are three ways out of check: move the king, block the attack, or capture the attacking piece.

exercises.title: Move away
exercises.prompt: Your king is in check. Move it to safety.
exercises.good: Any square off the e-file is safe.
exercises.bad: The rook attacks the whole e-file, including e2.

exercises.title: Block
exercises.prompt: Block the check with your bishop.
exercises.good: The bishop now stands between the rook and your king.
exercises.bad: Put the bishop on the e-file, between the rook and the king.

exercises.title: Capture
exercises.prompt: Capture the piece giving check.
exercises.good: Removing the attacker is often the best escape.
exercises.bad: Your knight can reach e8.

exercises.title: Find the escape
exercises.prompt: Which move gets out of check?
exercises.good: Qe2 blocks the e-file.
exercises.bad: The check comes down the e-file. Something has to land on it.

exercises.title: Checkmate
exercises.text: Checkmate is check with no way out: the king can't move, the check can't be blocked, and the attacker can't be captured. Checkmate ends the game.

exercises.title: The back-rank trap
exercises.text: A king behind its own unmoved pawns has no escape squares. A rook or queen landing on the back rank can deliver mate.

exercises.title: Mate in one
exercises.prompt: Deliver checkmate.
exercises.good: Ra8 is mate. The pawns block their own king.
exercises.bad: Aim your rook at the 8th rank.

exercises.title: Mate in one
exercises.prompt: Checkmate in one move.
exercises.good: Rxd8 is mate: nothing defended the rook on d8.
exercises.bad: The black rook on d8 is undefended.

exercises.title: Queen mate
exercises.prompt: Checkmate with the queen.
exercises.good: Qe8 mate. Same pattern, different piece.
exercises.bad: The e-file is open to the 8th rank.

exercises.title: Make a window
exercises.prompt: You are Black. White threatens Ra8 mate. Push a pawn to give your king an escape square.
exercises.good: Now your king has a square to run to. Players call this a luft.
exercises.bad: Move one of the three pawns in front of your king.

exercises.title: King and queen
exercises.text: A queen mates easily with the king's help: put the queen right next to the enemy king, protected by your own king.

exercises.title: Mate in one
exercises.prompt: Checkmate.
exercises.good: Qg7 mate. Your king protects the queen.
exercises.bad: Put the queen next to the black king on a square your king covers.

exercises.title: Mate in one
exercises.prompt: Checkmate along the back rank.
exercises.good: Qh8 mate. Your king covers a7 and b7.
exercises.bad: The 8th rank is open from h8.

exercises.title: Which one mates?
exercises.prompt: Which move is checkmate?
exercises.good: Qg7 is protected by your king, so the black king is stuck.
exercises.bad: After the check, can the black king capture or escape?

exercises.title: Mate in one
exercises.prompt: Checkmate.
exercises.good: Mate.
exercises.bad: Your king already covers the squares around h8 except the corner file.

exercises.title: Stalemate
exercises.text: Stalemate: the side to move is not in check but has no legal move. The game is a draw, even if the other side is far ahead.

exercises.title: Spot the trap
exercises.prompt: One of these moves throws away the win. Which move is stalemate?
exercises.good: After Qf7 Black has no legal move and isn't in check: a draw.
exercises.bad: Which move leaves the king with no moves and no check?

exercises.title: Finish properly
exercises.prompt: Now deliver checkmate instead.
exercises.good: Mate, not stalemate.
exercises.bad: Give check on the back rank.

exercises.title: What is this?
exercises.prompt: Black to move. What has happened?
exercises.good: Stalemate: the black king has no moves but is not in check.
exercises.bad: Is the black king attacked right now?

exercises.title: Careful
exercises.prompt: Mate in one. One wrong queen move is stalemate.
exercises.good: Qc8 mate.
exercises.bad: Check on the back rank. Your king covers a7 and b7.

exercises.title: Mate in one
exercises.prompt: Checkmate with the rook.
exercises.good: Ra8 mate.
exercises.bad: Your king covers the 7th rank. Use the back rank.

exercises.title: Mate in one
exercises.prompt: Checkmate with the rook.
exercises.good: Rh8 mate.
exercises.bad: Check along the 8th rank.

exercises.title: What is this?
exercises.prompt: Black to move. What has happened?
exercises.good: Checkmate. The king is attacked and has nowhere to go.
exercises.bad: Is the king attacked? Can it escape?

exercises.title: Escape
exercises.prompt: You are in check. Get out of it.
exercises.good: Safe.
exercises.bad: The rook attacks the 1st rank.

exercises.title: Mate in one
exercises.prompt: Checkmate with the queen.
exercises.good: Mate.
exercises.bad: Use the 8th rank.

exercises.title: The fork
exercises.text: A fork is one piece attacking two at once. Your opponent can only save one of them.

exercises.title: Knight fork
exercises.prompt: Fork the king and the rook.
exercises.good: Nc7+ hits the king and the rook. After the king moves, the rook falls.
exercises.bad: Find a square that attacks both e8 and a8.

exercises.title: Find the fork
exercises.prompt: Move the knight to a square where it attacks the king and the rook at the same time.
exercises.good: Nf7+ checks the king on h8 and hits the rook on d8.
exercises.bad: You need a square that reaches both h8 and d8.

exercises.title: Pawn fork
exercises.prompt: Even a pawn can fork. Attack both black pieces.
exercises.good: d4 attacks the knight and the rook. One of them is lost.
exercises.bad: A pawn attacks the two squares diagonally in front of it.

exercises.title: Which square?
exercises.prompt: Which knight move forks king and rook?
exercises.good: From c7 the knight reaches both a8 and e8.
exercises.bad: Check which squares each move attacks.

exercises.title: Queen fork
exercises.prompt: Fork the king and rook with your queen.
exercises.good: Qd5+ checks along one diagonal and hits the rook along the other. Nothing can take the queen.
exercises.bad: Find one square that sees both g8 and a8 on diagonals.

exercises.title: The pin
exercises.text: A pin attacks a piece that can't move away because a more valuable piece is behind it. When the king is behind, the pinned piece can't legally move at all.

exercises.title: Can it move?
exercises.prompt: Can the black knight on d7 move?
exercises.good: No. Moving it would expose the king to the bishop.
exercises.bad: What is behind the knight on the diagonal?

exercises.title: Make a pin
exercises.prompt: Pin the knight to the king.
exercises.good: Bb5 pins the knight.
exercises.bad: Put the bishop on the diagonal that runs through d7 to e8.

exercises.title: Spot the pin
exercises.prompt: Tap the pinned black piece.
exercises.good: The knight on c6 is pinned against the king.
exercises.bad: Follow the bishop's diagonal toward the black king.

exercises.title: Attack the pinned piece
exercises.prompt: The knight can't move. Attack it with a pawn.
exercises.good: d5 attacks the pinned knight, and it can't run.
exercises.bad: A pawn on d5 would attack c6.

exercises.title: The skewer
exercises.text: A skewer is a pin in reverse: the valuable piece is in front. When it moves out of the way, the piece behind it falls.

exercises.title: Skewer
exercises.prompt: Check the king so that the queen behind it is exposed.
exercises.good: Ra1+. The king must step aside and Rxa8 follows.
exercises.bad: Line up your rook with the king and queen on the a-file.

exercises.title: Skewer
exercises.prompt: Skewer the king and queen along the 5th rank.
exercises.good: Rh5+ and the queen on a5 drops.
exercises.bad: Check on the 5th rank from the side.

exercises.title: Name it
exercises.prompt: The bishop attacks the king, with the queen behind it. What is this?
exercises.good: Skewer: the more valuable piece is in front.
exercises.bad: Is the more valuable piece in front or behind?

exercises.title: Loose pieces
exercises.text: A hanging piece is attacked and not defended. Before every move, check what your opponent left loose and what you are leaving loose.

exercises.title: Find it
exercises.prompt: Tap the black piece your knight can capture for free.
exercises.good: The queen on d4 has no defender.
exercises.bad: Trace the knight's jumps from f3.

exercises.title: Take it
exercises.prompt: Capture the queen.
exercises.good: That is 9 points of material.
exercises.bad: Your knight reaches d4.

exercises.title: Find it
exercises.prompt: Tap the black piece your queen can win for free.
exercises.good: The knight on c6 is undefended. The f7 pawn is guarded by the king.
exercises.bad: Look along the queen's diagonals and files.

exercises.title: Take it
exercises.prompt: Win the knight.
exercises.good: A free piece.
exercises.bad: The diagonal from f3 runs to c6.

exercises.title: Free rook
exercises.prompt: Black left the rook on a8 undefended. Take it.
exercises.good: And it is even checkmate.
exercises.bad: Your rook and theirs share the a-file.

exercises.title: Fork
exercises.prompt: Fork the king and the rook.
exercises.good: Nd6+ forks e8 and c8.
exercises.bad: Find one square that attacks both c8 and e8.

exercises.title: Pin
exercises.prompt: Pin the knight to the king.
exercises.good: Bh5 pins the knight on f7.
exercises.bad: The diagonal from h5 runs through f7 to e8.

exercises.title: Skewer
exercises.prompt: Win the queen with a skewer.
exercises.good: Rh5+ wins the queen.
exercises.bad: Check along the 5th rank.

exercises.title: Hanging piece
exercises.prompt: Win the undefended piece.
exercises.good: Free bishop.
exercises.bad: Your rook and the bishop share a file.

exercises.title: Name it
exercises.prompt: What tactic is the knight on c7 using?
exercises.good: A fork: one piece, two targets.
exercises.bad: How many black pieces does the knight attack?

exercises.title: The centre
exercises.text: The four middle squares (d4, e4, d5, e5) are the centre. Pieces there control more of the board, so both sides fight for them from move one.

exercises.title: First move
exercises.prompt: Which first move fights for the centre?
exercises.good: e4 takes space in the centre and opens lines for the bishop and queen.
exercises.bad: Which pawn move reaches the middle of the board?

exercises.title: Claim the centre
exercises.prompt: Move your d-pawn two squares.
exercises.good: d4 grabs the centre.
exercises.bad: Push the pawn in front of the queen.

exercises.title: Black replies
exercises.prompt: Black to move. Which reply contests the centre?
exercises.good: ...e5 meets White in the centre on equal terms.
exercises.bad: Which move puts a pawn in the middle?

exercises.title: Centre in action
exercises.intro: Pieces placed in or aimed at the center control more squares and can reach either side of the board quickly. Fighting for central squares (d4/d5/e4/e5) is priority one in the early midgame.
exercises.completion: Central control is the foundation everything else in the middlegame is built on.

steps.note: White's bishop joins the fight for the center and aims at f7. In the midgame, almost every move should improve control of the center or your piece activity.

exercises.title: Develop
exercises.text: Development means bringing knights and bishops off the back rank early, toward the centre. Knights usually belong on f3 and c3.

exercises.title: Develop a knight
exercises.prompt: Develop a knight toward the centre and attack the e5 pawn.
exercises.good: Nf3 develops and attacks e5.
exercises.bad: The g1 knight can reach a square that hits e5.

exercises.title: Next piece
exercises.prompt: Which move develops a new minor piece?
exercises.good: Bc4 brings a bishop into play, aiming at f7.
exercises.bad: Knights and bishops are the minor pieces.

exercises.title: Queen early?
exercises.prompt: Why not bring the queen out on move two?
options: It gets chased by smaller pieces and you lose time
The queen can't move in the opening
exercises.good: Every time your queen is attacked you spend a move running instead of developing.
exercises.bad: Think about what happens when knights and bishops attack her.

exercises.title: Develop
exercises.prompt: Develop a knight.
exercises.good: Good. Knights first is a solid habit.
exercises.bad: Either knight toward the centre works.

exercises.title: Castling
exercises.text: Castling moves the king two squares toward a rook, and the rook hops over it. It tucks the king away and brings the rook toward the centre. Neither piece may have moved, the squares between must be empty, and the king can't be in check or pass through an attacked square.

exercises.title: Castle
exercises.prompt: Castle kingside: move the king two squares toward the h-rook.
exercises.good: Castled. Your king is safe behind its pawns.
exercises.bad: Move the king from e1 to g1.

exercises.title: Can you castle?
exercises.prompt: Can White castle right now?
exercises.good: No. You can't castle out of check.
exercises.bad: Is the white king attacked?

exercises.title: Which side?
exercises.prompt: The bishop on c4 watches f1. Which castling is legal?
exercises.good: Queenside. The king can't pass through f1 while the bishop attacks it.
exercises.bad: The king may not cross an attacked square.

exercises.title: Castle queenside
exercises.prompt: Castle queenside: move the king two squares toward the a-rook.
exercises.good: Castled long.
exercises.bad: Move the king from e1 to c1.

exercises.title: The Italian Game
exercises.text: One of the oldest openings. Both sides fight for the centre and develop toward it. You will play both sides, move by move.

exercises.title: Italian Game
exercises.intro: One of the oldest openings in chess. Both sides fight for the center and develop their pieces toward the action.
exercises.completion: You just played the Italian Game — a great first opening because every move has a clear purpose.

steps.note: White opens with the King's Pawn, claiming central space and opening lines for the bishop and queen.
Black mirrors immediately, contesting the center on equal terms.
White develops a knight that attacks e5 and prepares to castle.
Black defends e5 and develops a piece of their own — good chess is rarely one-sided.
White's bishop swings to c4, eyeing the weak f7 square — this is the Italian Game.
Black answers in kind, completing a harmonious, mirrored setup.

exercises.title: The Queen's Gambit
exercises.text: White offers a pawn to pull Black's centre pawn away. Black declines and keeps a solid centre. You play both sides.

exercises.title: Queen's Gambit Declined
exercises.intro: White offers a pawn to gain central control and faster development. Black politely declines and holds the center instead.
exercises.completion: You've played the classical Queen's Gambit Declined — one of the most rock-solid defenses in chess.

steps.note: White claims the center with the queen pawn.
Black answers symmetrically.
White offers the c-pawn — if Black grabs it, White gets quick development. This is the Queen's Gambit.
Black declines the gambit, reinforcing d5 instead of grabbing the pawn.
White develops naturally, keeping the center solid.

exercises.title: Open
exercises.prompt: Open with the king's pawn, two squares.
exercises.good: A classic first move.
exercises.bad: The pawn in front of the king.

exercises.title: Develop
exercises.prompt: Develop a knight.
exercises.good: Developed.
exercises.bad: Bring a knight toward the centre.

exercises.title: King safety
exercises.prompt: Castle kingside.
exercises.good: Safe king, active rook.
exercises.bad: King from e1 to g1.

exercises.title: The centre
exercises.prompt: Which four squares make up the centre?
exercises.good: Right.
exercises.bad: The very middle of the board.

exercises.title: Castling rule
exercises.prompt: Can White castle?
exercises.good: Not while in check.
exercises.bad: Look at the e-file.

exercises.title: The square rule
exercises.text: Can a king catch a passed pawn? Picture a square from the pawn to its promotion square. If the king can step into it, it catches the pawn.

exercises.title: Catch it?
exercises.prompt: White to move. Can the white king catch the pawn?
exercises.good: Yes. The king is inside the square a5–e5–e1–a1.
exercises.bad: Picture the square from a5 down to a1.

exercises.title: Catch it?
exercises.prompt: White to move. Can the white king catch the pawn now?
exercises.good: No. The king on g1 is outside the square and the pawn promotes.
exercises.bad: Is g1 inside the square a5–e5–e1–a1?

exercises.title: Chase
exercises.prompt: Head toward the pawn.
exercises.good: Right direction. You stay inside the square.
exercises.bad: Move the king toward a1.

exercises.title: The Square Rule
exercises.intro: To know if a passed pawn can outrun the enemy king, picture a square from the pawn to the promotion square. If the defending king is already inside that square, it can catch the pawn; if not, the pawn runs home alone.
exercises.completion: The square rule turns "is this pawn fast enough?" into something you can check at a glance.

steps.note: Black's king on h8 is far outside the square from e5 to e8 — this pawn cannot be caught.
Black tries anyway...
...but the pawn is simply faster.
One step too slow.
The pawn promotes untouched. Always check the square rule before assuming a passed pawn is dangerous — or safe.

exercises.title: The technique
exercises.text: Use the queen to shrink the king's box, bring your own king close, then mate on the edge. Watch for stalemate every move.

exercises.title: Mate in one
exercises.prompt: Checkmate.
exercises.good: Mate.
exercises.bad: Check on the 8th rank, or next to the king where yours protects.

exercises.title: Mate in one
exercises.prompt: Checkmate.
exercises.good: Mate in the corner.
exercises.bad: The black king is stuck on the first rank.

exercises.title: King + Queen vs King
exercises.intro: The most basic winning endgame: queen and king cooperate to box the enemy king into a corner or edge, where it eventually runs out of squares.
exercises.completion: Bring your king up to help, rather than trying to mate with the queen alone — it is faster and safer.

steps.note: The queen delivers mate along the back rank, while White's king nearby cuts off every nearby escape square — queen and king always work as a team.

exercises.title: The rook wall
exercises.text: A rook can cut the enemy king off along a rank or file. Push the king to the edge, then mate with king and rook together.

exercises.title: Cutting Off the King with a Rook
exercises.intro: In rook endgames, a rook placed on the right rank or file can completely block the enemy king from reaching the action on the other side of the board.
exercises.completion: A rook on an active rank or file is often worth more than grabbing a pawn immediately.

steps.note: The rook moves to an active rank, cutting Black's king off from advancing further — a core rook-endgame technique you'll use constantly.

exercises.title: Opposition
exercises.text: Kings standing on the same file with one square between them are in opposition. The side that does not have to move holds it, and the other king must give way.

exercises.title: Take it
exercises.prompt: Which king move takes the opposition?
exercises.good: Kd4: one square between the kings, and Black must move.
exercises.bad: Face the black king with exactly one square between.

exercises.title: Take it
exercises.prompt: Take the opposition.
exercises.good: Ke4. Now Black has to give ground.
exercises.bad: Step forward so only one square separates the kings.

exercises.title: Beware of stalemate
exercises.intro: A position is a stalemate — an immediate draw — if the side to move has no legal moves and is not in check. It is one of the most common ways to throw away a completely winning position.
exercises.completion: Before your final move in a won endgame, always ask: does my opponent have any legal move left at all?

steps.note: This looks like progress, but check carefully: Black's king on h8 has no legal moves (g8, g7 and h7 are all covered) and is not in check. That's a stalemate — a draw, not a win!
